title: NFS Mount Stale Handle Detection
exclusions: Detects only indexed Linux system or application records containing the exact user-space error text `Stale file handle` / `Stale NFS file handle`, the NFSv3 or NFSv4 file-handle statuses `NFS3ERR_STALE` / `NFS4ERR_STALE`, or `ESTALE` within 160 characters of `NFS`. It deliberately excludes generic words such as `stale`, NFS server timeout/recovery messages, `NFS4ERR_STALE_CLIENTID`, `NFS4ERR_STALE_STATEID`, stale attribute-cache discussions, and errors that were returned to an application but never logged. A generic `Stale file handle` line does not by itself prove that the affected filesystem is NFS because Linux documents ESTALE for other filesystems too. The search does not discover the mount point or server when the emitting record omits them, test mount availability, identify the invalidating server-side change, repair or remount a filesystem, or provide regulatory attestation. The base SPL applies no exception lookup.
evidence: After deployment, retain the `linux_nfs_stale_file_handle_5m` saved-search definition and schedule, dispatch and alert history, the matching raw record, result fields (`_time`, `host`, `first_seen`, `last_seen`, `event_count`, `signature_classes`, `sourcetypes`, `sources`, `processes`), effective Universal Forwarder monitor configuration, and dated positive/negative control-test output. Link the alert to a host-side `findmnt` or equivalent capture and the incident or approved maintenance record when available. These artifacts show that collected text matched this rule; they do not prove continuous log coverage, NFS attribution for a generic strerror line, or production validation.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index, ingest two events for `host=nfs-client-test` in the same five-minute bucket: `backup[412]: open /srv/share/report failed: Stale file handle` and `nfs-probe[413]: server=files01 export=/data status=NFS4ERR_STALE`. Run a copy of the SPL with fixed time bounds and the test index substituted for `os`. Expect exactly one result with `event_count=2`, `signature_classes` containing `generic_stale_handle_text` and `nfs_protocol_status`, both test sources represented, and the original event times retained in `first_seen` and `last_seen`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Ingest `kernel: NFS: server files01 not responding, still trying`, `kernel: NFS: server files01 OK`, `nfs-client: NFS4ERR_STALE_CLIENTID after server restart`, `nfs-client: NFS4ERR_STALE_STATEID during recovery`, and `cache-agent: stale attribute cache refreshed` in the same fixed window. Expect zero results. Also ingest `worker: ESTALE while opening local object` without `NFS`; it must not match, proving that bare symbolic errno text is not attributed to NFS without nearby NFS context.

dataSources: Line-oriented logs from Linux NFS client workloads routed to the deployment's operating-system event index, called `index=os` in this record. Monitor the distribution text log that actually receives service or application errors (commonly `/var/log/messages` or `/var/log/syslog`) as `sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog`, and separately monitor an in-scope application's own error log when it does not write to syslog, assigning a stable source type appropriate to that format. Required Splunk fields are `_time`, `host`, `_raw`, `source`, and `sourcetype`; `process` is optional. The Linux NFS client returns ESTALE to the calling process and does not guarantee a kernel log line, so collection must cover the process that renders or records the error. The search intentionally spans source types inside the controlled `os` index.
app: Splunk Universal Forwarder native file-monitor inputs and built-in `linux_messages_syslog` parsing where applicable. Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) is optional deployment context for `/var/log` collection and NFS performance telemetry; its `nfsiostat.sh` scripted input does not collect stale-file-handle error events.

splunkbaseApps.name: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux

spl:
index=os ("Stale file handle" OR "Stale NFS file handle" OR "NFS3ERR_STALE" OR "NFS4ERR_STALE" OR (NFS ESTALE))
| rex field=_raw "(?i)(?<stale_signature>\bNFS(?:3|4)ERR_STALE\b|stale\s+NFS\s+file\s+handle|stale\s+file\s+handle|\bNFS\b.{0,160}\bESTALE\b|\bESTALE\b.{0,160}\bNFS\b)"
| where isnotnull(stale_signature)
| eval signature_class=case(match(stale_signature,"(?i)^NFS[34]ERR_STALE$"),"nfs_protocol_status",match(stale_signature,"(?i)^stale NFS"),"explicit_nfs_text",match(stale_signature,"(?i)ESTALE"),"nfs_context_errno",true(),"generic_stale_handle_text"), event_time=_time
| bin _time span=5m
| stats min(event_time) as first_seen max(event_time) as last_seen count as event_count values(signature_class) as signature_classes values(sourcetype) as sourcetypes values(source) as sources values(process) as processes first(_raw) as sample_event by _time host
| sort 0 -_time host
description: Detects canonical stale-file-handle error text and NFS protocol status names in indexed Linux client workload logs, while rejecting broad `stale` matches and similarly named NFSv4 client/state recovery errors. It returns one row per host and five-minute bucket with the matching-record count, signature classes, source types, source paths, optional processes, and one raw example for triage.
value: Detecting stale NFS handles promptly helps Linux, application, and storage owners prevent repeated reads, writes, traversal, backup, build, or database failures from widening an outage. Source-preserving evidence improves identification of the affected path and server-side change even when the mount remains present.
implementation: Collect the logs of processes that can encounter ESTALE, because the Linux NFS client returns the error to the caller and a kernel message is not guaranteed. Search only canonical stale-handle text or NFS file-handle status tokens, schedule over a completed five-minute bucket, and alert on any result. Validate the matched host and path against current NFS mounts before attribution; one exact record is the initial actionable threshold, not a vendor-prescribed count.
visualization: Use a critical latest-first table with bucket time, host, first and last event time, event count, signature classes, processes, source types, and source paths, with drilldown to `sample_event` and surrounding application records. Add a 24-hour recurrence chart by host and a separate collection-freshness panel for each expected log source. Do not display an `nfs_server` or mount-point column unless a locally validated parser or inventory enrichment actually supplies it.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. CIM has no documented normalized field for these raw NFS/user-space error signatures, and server, export, mount point, and process are not uniformly present. No equivalent accelerated `tstats` search is claimed.

knownFalsePositives:
A canonical match normally represents a real failed operation or protocol status. The false-positive question is whether it belongs to the intended NFS production scope and whether a new notification is useful:

1. **Approved export replacement or storage migration** — Recreating an exported filesystem, changing export identity, or another controlled cutover can invalidate handles held by active clients. Confirm the exact client fleet, export, change ticket, and bounded maintenance window; retain the matches as change evidence and suppress only notification actions for that window.

2. **Expected delete/recreate race in a disposable workflow** — A backup crawler, build cleanup, or batch worker may hold an old handle after another actor replaces an object. The error is genuine even if retry succeeds. Confirm the path, application retry result, and owner-approved behavior before downgrading; repeated errors still indicate a concurrency or workflow defect.

3. **Non-NFS ESTALE rendered as `Stale file handle`** — Linux explicitly allows ESTALE for other filesystems. A generic strerror line without protocol, server, export, or path context is only a candidate. Use `findmnt -T <path>` or an equivalent namespace-aware check on the same host; if the path is not on NFS, correct routing or add a more specific source-local filter rather than suppressing every generic signature.

4. **Synthetic health check or resilience exercise** — A test harness may intentionally log `NFS3ERR_STALE`, `NFS4ERR_STALE`, or `Stale file handle`. Require a named test host/process, approved start and end, and exercise identifier. Never suppress by message text alone because production applications emit the same text.

5. **Duplicate file and syslog collection** — One application record can be indexed from its own file and again through `/var/log/messages`, inflating `event_count` and causing duplicate pages. Compare source paths, `_raw`, event time, and `_indextime`; remove overlapping collection while preserving one authoritative feed.

6. **Forwarder backlog or replay** — A historical stale-handle record delivered after a forwarder restart can open a new page after the underlying issue ended. Compare `_time` with `_indextime`, current mount identity, and prior incidents. Retain the delayed event but close or downgrade the duplicate notification.

**Safe suppression:** the primary SPL has no hidden allow-list. If local policy requires alert-action suppression, use a separately tested lookup keyed by exact `host` and, only when reliably extracted, `source` or process, with `valid_from`, `valid_until`, `ticket`, `owner`, and `reason`. Reject wildcards and non-expiring entries, apply suppression after the base result, and preserve suppressed matches for review.
reviewer: documentation review against IETF NFS, Linux kernel/client, Linux man-pages, and Splunk primary sources; no runtime execution or SME sign-off
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and signal semantics

Assign a Linux/NFS client owner, the owner of each workload whose logs are in scope, a storage or NFS server escalation owner, and a Splunk content owner. A Universal Forwarder or another approved file-forwarding tier must be able to read the selected text logs and send them through the deployment's existing secured route. The search role needs read access to the operating-system event index and permission to schedule the alert; no root access, NFS server credential, premium Splunk app, or custom polling script is required by this detection. This record calls the event index `os`, but that is a local convention and must be changed consistently if the deployment uses another name.

Understand the boundary before collecting data. RFC 1813 defines `NFS3ERR_STALE` as an invalid file handle whose object no longer exists or whose access was revoked. RFC 8881 defines `NFS4ERR_STALE` for a filehandle that is no longer valid, including a removed object or unavailable filesystem. Linux maps the protocol status to `ESTALE`; the normal error text is `Stale file handle`. The Linux errno documentation also says ESTALE can occur on other filesystems, so a generic text line is a high-value candidate, not proof of NFS attribution. `NFS4ERR_STALE_CLIENTID` and `NFS4ERR_STALE_STATEID` describe different NFSv4 recovery state and are intentionally excluded.

The client-side logging model is equally important. The NFS client returns the error to the system call made by the workload. The kernel is not required to emit a persistent text record for every returned ESTALE. This use case therefore detects only callers, service managers, probes, or libraries that write the error into a collected log. `journalctl -k`, a generic kernel log, or the Unix add-on's `nfsiostat.sh` cannot be assumed to contain application failures. Document which process logs are covered and create a separate collection-health control; absence of stale-handle matches is meaningful only while those logs are current.

## Step 1 — Configure and qualify collection

Inventory workloads that read or write NFS mounts and identify where each one records failed file operations. If a service writes through syslog into the distribution's active `/var/log/messages` or `/var/log/syslog`, use Splunk's native file monitor and the pretrained `linux_messages_syslog` source type. If the application has a dedicated line-oriented error log, monitor that exact file with a source type tested for its timestamp and event boundaries. Do not label arbitrary application formats as `linux_messages_syslog`, do not monitor the binary systemd journal as a flat file, and do not collect every `/var/log` path when a narrower source is sufficient.

Package monitor stanzas in a managed deployment app or the approved local directory; never edit a vendor app's `default` files. A representative syslog input is:

```ini
[monitor:///var/log/messages]
disabled = 0
index = os
sourcetype = linux_messages_syslog
```

Use the path that actually receives the workload's error on that operating-system image. For a dedicated application log, create a separate monitor stanza and assign its validated source type. Follow least privilege: grant the forwarder account read and directory-traverse access only where needed. After deployment or restart, use `splunk btool inputs list --debug` to verify the winning stanza and its origin. Search `index=os host=<test-client> earliest=-15m` and inspect `_time`, `host`, `_raw`, `source`, and `sourcetype`; verify that an ordinary application record has one event, the correct timestamp, and stable host identity. If a parser extracts `process`, treat it as optional enrichment, not a grouping prerequisite.

Capture normal event and byte volume by `host,source` before broad rollout. The detection itself is rare, but license and storage cost come from the complete application and system logs. Check rotation and forwarding delay, prevent duplicate local-file and syslog-relay collection, and build a freshness panel for every expected source. The optional `Splunk_TA_nix` deployment can support broader `/var/log` and `nfsiostat.sh` telemetry, but the add-on's documented scripted-input inventory does not contain a stale-handle collector; do not represent `nfsiostat` counters as error events.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the search

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_nfs_stale_file_handle_5m`. The base terms select exact user-visible phrases, exact protocol status names, or events containing both `NFS` and `ESTALE`. `rex` then enforces the real signature boundary. Its word boundaries prevent `NFS4ERR_STALE_CLIENTID` and `NFS4ERR_STALE_STATEID` from being accepted as `NFS4ERR_STALE`; the 160-character proximity rule prevents a bare ESTALE token from being attributed to NFS solely because the host happens to mount NFS elsewhere. `where` removes base-search candidates that fail this second-stage expression.

`signature_class` distinguishes protocol statuses, explicitly NFS-labelled text, NFS-context symbolic errno, and generic user-space strerror text. The original `_time` is copied before five-minute bucketing. `stats` returns one result per bucket and host, retaining first and last event times, matching indexed-record count, source types, source paths, any extracted processes, and one unmodified sample. `event_count` is not a count of distinct files, handles, failed system calls, or affected applications; duplicate ingestion can increase it. The SPL does not fabricate `nfs_server`, `mountpoint`, or export fields because none is guaranteed in these messages.

Run the search every five minutes over a completed bucket, initially `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`, after measuring that a five-minute delay covers normal ingestion latency. Trigger when the result count is greater than zero. One canonical record is the initial threshold because it represents at least one failed operation or explicit protocol status; there is no IETF, Linux, or Splunk vendor count threshold. Route a single generic line according to workload criticality and confirmation confidence rather than automatically declaring a fleet-wide critical outage. Deduplicate notification actions by host and source for a short policy-approved period such as 30 minutes, but preserve every dispatch and avoid a host-only suppression that could hide a second application.

There is no honest CIM or `tstats` equivalent. These fields are extracted from raw text, and message producers do not consistently include server, export, mount, path, or process. Add local enrichment only after testing it against each producer. If an event includes a path, responders can resolve its current filesystem with a namespace-aware `findmnt -T <path>` check; that live result provides context but cannot prove what was mounted when a delayed historical event occurred.

## Step 3 — Validate signatures and collection coverage

Use an isolated test index and fixed earliest/latest bounds. Index the two positive records in `controlTest` with the same timestamp parsing and host metadata as production. They must collapse into one host/bucket result with `event_count=2` and both expected signature classes. Verify `first_seen`, `last_seen`, sources, source types, and `sample_event`, not only result count. Repeat each accepted form separately: lowercase `stale file handle`, `Stale NFS file handle`, `NFS3ERR_STALE`, `NFS4ERR_STALE`, `NFS ... ESTALE`, and `ESTALE ... NFS` within the proximity limit.

Run the negative scenario exactly. Server timeout and recovery messages are availability signals, not stale file handles. `NFS4ERR_STALE_CLIENTID` and `NFS4ERR_STALE_STATEID` must be rejected despite sharing a prefix. A bare `ESTALE` without nearby NFS and a generic `stale attribute cache` line must also be rejected. Add boundary tests with NFS and ESTALE more than 160 characters apart and with the two tokens in either order. Duplicate one accepted record under two source paths and confirm `event_count=2`; this demonstrates why count is not a severity threshold.

For collection acceptance, use a disposable application or test harness that calls its normal logging path with the literal error text; do not delete or replace a production export merely to make handles stale. Confirm the source record, forwarded event, search dispatch, alert action, and end-to-end latency. If the platform team has a separately approved disposable NFS fault-injection procedure, capture the client kernel, NFS version, server/export identity, operation, exact returned/logged error, and cleanup. There is no common vendor UI for a generic Linux NFS mount; cross-reference the indexed record against the native client mount view and the authoritative application log instead of claiming a console comparison. This editorial review did not run such a procedure, index a fixture, or execute the SPL in Splunk, which is why the metadata remains `draft` and no Splunk version matrix is asserted.

## Step 4 — Operationalize response and evidence

Build a latest-first table containing the bucket, host, first and last occurrence, event count, signature classes, processes, source types, and source paths. Drill down to the raw record and surrounding application events. Add a recurrence chart by host and a separate source-freshness panel. Restrict raw-log access to the relevant operations roles because application records can contain paths, tenant identifiers, or job parameters. Route alerts first to the workload and Linux owners, with storage/NFS server escalation after client-side confirmation; this is an operational fault, not inherently a security incident.

The response runbook should preserve the exact message, determine the emitting process and failed operation, and extract the path only if the record supplies it. In the same mount namespace as the workload, use `findmnt -T <path>` or approved platform tooling to confirm current `nfs`/`nfs4` type, source, target, and options. For containerized workloads, host-namespace mount output may differ and must not be treated as authoritative. Correlate the event with server/export maintenance, filesystem replacement, snapshots or failover, file deletion/recreation, application deployment, and nearby NFS availability errors. Check whether retries succeeded and whether the error affects one object, one export, or multiple clients.

Do not automatically run `umount`, `umount -l`, `mount -o remount`, kill processes, reboot clients, or change exports from this alert. A remount can disrupt active I/O and cannot restore a deleted object. Follow the storage and application owners' recovery procedure: quiesce or fail over the workload when required, verify server/export identity, remount only under change control, and restart or retry the affected process only when its consistency guarantees are understood. Retain the saved-search revision, effective input, matching record, test output, incident or change link, and disposition under the operations evidence policy.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot and suppress safely

If no events appear after a known application error, the process may have written only to stderr or journald, the wrong text file may be monitored, the forwarder may lack read permission, routing may use another index, timestamp extraction may have moved the event outside the window, or the search role may lack access. Fix the actual logging path; a kernel-only input cannot guarantee this signal. Events present but unmatched require comparing `_raw` with the canonical forms and upstream producer documentation. Add a signature only with positive and negative samples; do not restore the broad word `stale` or treat server-not-responding messages as equivalent.

If generic text matches a local filesystem, keep the evidence but correct the NFS attribution. If `nfs_server` or mount point is missing, that is expected unless the application logged it; do not create a field from the Splunk host name. Duplicate counts generally indicate overlapping file/syslog collection or replay after rotation. Late pages indicate forwarding backlog beyond the completed-bucket delay; compare `_time` and `_indextime`, repair the pipeline, and adjust delay from measured latency rather than widening the event window indefinitely.

For approved maintenance or testing, suppress only the alert action through an exact, expiring, owner-reviewed lookup after the base result. Require host, a reliably extracted source or process where available, start and end epochs, ticket, owner, and reason. Preserve suppressed matches and test expiration and missing-field behavior. Never suppress all `Stale file handle` text fleet-wide, use a wildcard host, or make an exception non-expiring, because the same canonical message can represent an unrelated production failure.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for programs saying that a shared network file or folder reference is no longer accepted. That warning helps the team find the affected storage connection before more jobs fail or important work is interrupted.
